explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 2 of Stage 8 Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. In Unit 1 you sharpened your first skill, Research: you learned to ask a question you could argue, gather information from a range of sources, cross-check them, and pull your findings together. That skill gave you good information. This unit teaches you what to do with it.

Remember that this subject grows six skills, and each one leans on the others:

This unit is about the second skill: Analysis. Research told you *what* is happening. Analysis asks the deeper questions: why is it happening, who sees it differently, what does it lead to, and how is it being framed? Good information is only raw material; analysis is how you turn it into understanding.

You already analyse, even if you have never used the word. When you work out why one market stall is always busier than the next, or why two friends remember the same argument in opposite ways, or why the price of fuel changes what your family eats, you are analysing. In Stage 8 you will do it far more deliberately, across several sources at once, about real issues in your community and the wider world.
bullets: Research — finding things out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — taking a topic apart to see its causes, its effects and the many ways people view it.
Evaluation — judging how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking honestly about how you learn and how your views change.
Collaboration — working well with other people towards a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas so clearly that others truly understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning the Ehel Academy way, which is self-paced. Three kinds of support work together, and in Stage 8 you take more of the lead yourself:

Analysis grows fastest through conversation, because its whole point is to see an issue from more than one side. Older versions of this subject told learners to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss with the class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So treat every 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box as a real debate: give your view, then ask the tutor to argue against it, and see whether your thinking still holds.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and work through each activity in your own time. Slow down where an idea is hard, such as telling a reasoned argument from a bare opinion; move quickly where it is easy.

Your AI tutor, available every hour of the day. Wherever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a thoughtful study partner and a whole class rolled into one. It discusses your ideas, argues the other side, and gives feedback whenever you are ready.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In live sessions you bring your best analysis and your sharpest questions, hear how other learners read the same issue, and get guidance on where to go next.

explainers.title: Meet Zane, our analyst for this unit
explainers.body:
To make every idea concrete, we will follow one Year 8 learner through the whole unit. His name is Zane, and he studies at Ehel Academy in Berbera, on the coast.

Zane's town has always lived with the sea. But lately the fishers come back to the harbour with less than they used to. His neighbour, an old fisher named Mr Diallo, says he now spends longer at sea for a smaller catch. At the market, fish sellers grumble that prices are rising; a cafe owner, Ms Chen, worries she cannot buy enough for her customers; and a younger fisher shrugs and says the sea has good years and bad years, nothing more. Zane notices that everyone describes the same harbour in a different way. He starts to wonder: why is the catch falling, who sees the problem differently, and what would actually help?

That question becomes Zane's project for this unit. Notice that he is no longer only *finding out* what is happening, as he would in Research. He is taking the issue apart: hunting for causes, following consequences onto other people, comparing the perspectives around the harbour, and reading the numbers in the catch records. As you meet each analysis skill, you will see exactly what Zane does with it, and you will do the very same thing with an issue that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
Just as in Research, this unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a real issue that matters where you live and also connects to the wider world. You keep returning to it, lesson after lesson, and each analysis skill adds another layer to your understanding of it.

You have a choice. You may keep the Challenge you researched in Unit 1 and now analyse it far more deeply, which is a strong option because you already have information and sources. Or you may choose a new issue if something else has caught your attention. Here are some issues that are very real across the Horn of Africa and rich with different perspectives:

The best issue for analysis is one where thoughtful people honestly disagree. If everyone already agrees on the cause and the cure, there is little left to analyse. So look for an issue where a market seller, a parent, a student, a business owner and a leader might each say something different, and each have a point.
bullets: Fewer fish along the coast, and the future of fishing near Berbera
Clean air and the growth of traffic in our towns
Growing towns and what happens to open land and wildlife
Cutting trees for charcoal, and what it does to the soil and the weather
Plastic waste on our streets and along the coast
Road safety on busy roads near schools
Girls staying in school to the end
Work and training for young people leaving school
Clean water and safe sanitation in the dry season

explainers.title: What is analysis, really?
explainers.body:
The word analysis means breaking something into its parts to understand it better. When you analyse an issue, you stop treating it as one solid lump and start asking careful questions about the pieces inside: What exactly is the problem? Why is it happening? What does it lead to, and for whom? Who is involved, and how does each of them see it? A useful way to remember the difference is this: research gathers the pieces, and analysis works out how the pieces fit together.

Good analysis brings together several kinds of thinking. In this unit you will practise each one:

That looks like a long list, but almost every part answers one of three plain questions: *What is going on? Why, and who sees it how? And so what should happen?* Keep those three questions in mind and analysis will feel natural.
bullets: Telling apart an issue, a perspective and a course of action.
Using the four perspective types: personal, local, national and global.
Identifying and comparing perspectives across several sources.
Sorting fact, opinion and reasoned argument.
Explaining causes and consequences, and following the chain onto others.
Reading and building data, such as a double-bar graph, to support an argument.
Identifying the stakeholders and gathering a group's perspective fairly.
Noticing how the framing of an issue shapes the way people see it.
Drawing a supported conclusion and justifying a course of action.

explainers.title: Keep an analysis journal
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first skill, start a habit that makes analysis far easier: keep an analysis journal. This is a notebook or a document where you build up your Challenge piece by piece. Each time you work, note the date, the source or person you drew on, and what you added: a cause, a consequence, a perspective, a number, a question you still have.

The journal matters for three reasons. It keeps all the pieces of your analysis in one place, so you can see the whole issue at once. It shows how your thinking changes as you learn more, which you will need for Reflection. And it makes your final conclusion far easier to write, because the evidence is already gathered and sorted. Keep it beside you as you read on.

explainers.title: Skill 1 (2.1): Issue, perspective and course of action
explainers.body:
Three words sit at the very centre of Analysis, and Stage 8 asks you to tell them apart clearly: issue, perspective and course of action.

Keeping these three apart stops a lot of muddled thinking. The issue is the problem itself. A perspective is not the problem; it is one way of seeing it, and a single issue can be seen through many perspectives at once. A course of action is not a view at all; it is a step, a plan, a thing to be done. A quick test: if people might say 'someone should do something about this', you have an issue; if you can put 'I think' or 'in our view' in front of it, you have a perspective; if it starts with a verb like 'organise', 'ask' or 'plant', it is a course of action.
bullets: An issue is an important topic or problem that people care about and that may need a solution. Fewer fish, waste, road safety and clean water are all issues.
A perspective is a way of looking at an issue: a point of view, shaped by who a person is, where they live, and what they value.
A course of action is something you could actually do to make a positive difference to the issue.

explainers.title: Skill 2 (2.1): The four perspectives - personal, local, national, global
explainers.body:
The same issue looks different depending on who is viewing it and how far away they stand. Stage 8 asks you to use four named perspectives, and to be precise about what each one really means. They are more than four distances; each has its own character.

A strong analyst moves between these four instead of getting stuck at one. Someone who only ever sees the personal level misses the bigger picture; someone who only talks about the global level forgets the real people next door. Notice too that a personal perspective is not the same as a bare opinion: it must be based on evidence, or it is only a feeling.
bullets: A personal perspective is what *you* think about an issue, formed after exploring other views and weighing the causes and consequences. Because it rests on evidence, it can grow or change as you learn more.
A local perspective is the view a particular *community* holds about an issue, not just facts about that community. It is often shaped by local leaders and local groups.
A national perspective is the view a whole *country* takes, usually seen in its laws, its policies, and the speeches of its politicians.
A global perspective is a view whose influence spreads *beyond any single country*. It may come from a country, an organisation or even one person, but it reaches across the world.

explainers.title: Skill 3 (2.1): Comparing perspectives across several sources
explainers.body:
In Stage 8 you rarely rely on one source. Instead you gather ideas and evidence from different perspectives within different sources, then place them side by side and compare. The goal is to build a fair map of who thinks what, and what evidence each side offers, before you decide anything yourself.

When you compare several sources, look for three things: where they agree, where they disagree, and what each one leaves out. That last point is often the most revealing, because a source usually stays silent about the parts that do not suit its perspective. Watching for the silence is a mark of a careful analyst.

explainers.title: Skill 4 (2.1): Fact, opinion and reasoned argument
explainers.body:
When you analyse what people say and write, you must sort three different kinds of statement. Telling them apart is one of the most useful analysis skills of all.

All three matter, but they carry different weight. A reasoned argument is far stronger than a bare opinion, because you can test its reasons and check its evidence. This is the difference between 'the sea is empty' (an opinion) and 'the catch has halved in five years because there are twice as many boats, and the young fish are netted before they breed' (a reasoned argument). The second gives you something you can actually examine. A Stage 8 rule to remember: a perspective is only worth much when it is supported by evidence; otherwise it is just an opinion.
bullets: A fact is something that can be checked and shown to be true, such as a count, a measurement or a date.
An opinion is what someone thinks, feels or believes. It cannot simply be looked up, and others may honestly disagree.
A reasoned argument is an opinion backed by reasons and evidence. It says not only *what* someone thinks, but *why*, and offers facts to support it.

explainers.title: Skill 5 (2.3): Explaining causes and consequences on others
explainers.body:
At the heart of analysis is a pair of questions: why did this happen, and what does it lead to? The answers are causes and consequences. Stage 8 asks you to go further than naming one of each, and to follow the chain, showing how a consequence for one group becomes a cause of trouble for another.

Most issues have several causes and several consequences, and the consequences rarely stop with one person. One effect becomes the cause of the next, rippling out onto other people, which is exactly what the objective means by 'consequences on others'. Certain signal words help you spot and explain the links in what you read and write.
bullets: A cause is the reason why an event or situation happens or has happened.
A consequence is the result or effect of something that has happened or is happening.

explainers.title: Skill 6 (2.2): Reading and building data to support an argument
explainers.body:
Not all evidence is words. Some of the strongest evidence is data: numbers, counts and measurements, often shown in a bar graph. Stage 8 asks you both to read data and to build it yourself, and then to use it to support an argument. Numbers, presented clearly, can make a perspective far more convincing than feelings alone.

When you meet a graph, read it in a calm order: first the title (what is it about?), then the labels on each axis (what is counted, and in what units?), then the bars (which is tallest, which is shortest, and what is the overall pattern?). A double-bar graph is especially useful, because it lets you compare two groups side by side, such as two years, two seasons, or two landing sites. Whenever you present a graph, add a sentence or two of text to explain what it shows; a graph without words leaves the reader guessing.

explainers.title: Skill 7 (2.1): Stakeholders and gathering a group's perspective
explainers.body:
Every issue has people who care about it, and the word for them is stakeholders. A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue, because it affects them or they can affect it. A group of stakeholders often shares common knowledge and values, which shape a common perspective. Listing the stakeholders is one of the surest ways to check that you have not missed an important perspective.

Two ideas make this skill powerful. First, each stakeholder group tends to see the issue in its own way, because its members share what they know and value. Second, even within one group there can be different perspectives: two fishers, or two shopkeepers, may not agree. Never assume a whole group speaks with one voice.

explainers.title: Skill 8 (2.1): Noticing how an issue is framed
explainers.body:
Here is a subtle Stage 8 skill that many adults never learn. The very same issue can be framed, or worded, in different ways, and the framing quietly shapes how people react before they have thought at all. A careful analyst notices the frame and looks past it to the issue underneath.

Framing works by choosing which words to use and which facts to highlight. Call the same people 'greedy fishers' and you invite blame; call them 'struggling families' and you invite sympathy; call the situation 'an unmanaged resource' and you invite rules and planning. Nothing about the sea has changed, yet each frame points you towards a different feeling and a different course of action. Framing is closely tied to bias: a framed statement leans one way on purpose.

explainers.title: Skill 9 (2.4): Drawing a conclusion and justifying a course of action
explainers.body:
All of your analysis builds towards two things: a conclusion you can support with evidence, and a course of action you can justify. A conclusion is not your first feeling. It is a careful judgement reached *after* weighing the causes, the consequences, the data and the different perspectives, fairly and evenly.

Before you decide what to do, Stage 8 asks you to question your way towards a sensible action. A useful set of questions uses the words What, Why, Who, Which, When and How:

explainers.title: Staying fair when you analyse
explainers.body:
Analysis gives you the power to take an issue apart, so it also asks you to be fair. The heart of Global Perspectives is seeing an issue from many sides evenly, before you decide. A fair analyst listens to perspectives they disagree with just as carefully as ones they like, and weighs the evidence on every side.

People's perspectives are shaped by many things: where they live, what work they do, their age, their family, and their culture or beliefs. Noticing this helps you understand a viewpoint instead of dismissing it. And now that you can spot framing, you can catch yourself framing an issue to suit your own side, which is one of the most honest things a thinker can do.

explainers.title: How analysis links to the other five skills
explainers.body:
Analysis sits in the middle of the six skills, and it connects to every one of them. It takes what research gives you and prepares the way for everything that follows.

So the thinking you practise here is never wasted. Analysis is the bridge between simply knowing about an issue and being able to judge it, discuss it, and act on it wisely.
bullets: Research feeds analysis: you cannot break an issue into causes and perspectives until you have gathered good, cross-checked information.
Evaluation builds on analysis: once you can see the different views, evaluation helps you judge which arguments are actually strongest.
Reflection grows every time you notice how your analysis changed your mind about an issue.
Collaboration improves when you can understand other people's perspectives instead of only your own.
Communication becomes clearer and fairer when it rests on careful analysis rather than on a first reaction.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the analysis cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every analysis skill in this unit. Here is how they fit into one clear cycle you can use for any issue:
bullets: Name the issue clearly, and keep it apart from perspectives and courses of action.
View the issue through four perspectives: personal, local, national and global.
Gather perspectives across several sources, and sort fact, opinion and reasoned argument.
Map the causes and consequences, following the chain onto others.
Read and build data to spot patterns, and list the stakeholders.
Notice how the issue is framed, and restate it plainly.
Draw a conclusion supported by evidence, and justify a realistic course of action.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Evaluation. Once you can analyse an issue, breaking it into causes, consequences, data and perspectives, evaluation teaches you to weigh those perspectives and arguments and judge how strong each one really is. Strong analysis now will make strong evaluation much easier later. Well done for taking your thinking to a new level in Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to hold on to
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is the vehicle and the skill is the destination.
This unit travels through real issues such as the sea and its fish, growing towns, and clean air.
But the aim is not to become an expert on fishing. The aim is to become a thinker who can take almost any issue apart, weigh every side fairly, and reach a supported conclusion.

bigIdeas.title: Why the difference matters
lines: If you confuse a perspective with the issue, you end up arguing about a single opinion instead of studying the whole problem.
If you jump to a course of action before you understand the issue, your plan may fix the wrong thing.
Strong analysis names the issue first, gathers the perspectives, and only then works towards an action.

bigIdeas.title: How a local perspective takes shape
lines: A local perspective is a community's shared view, often supported by local groups and leaders.
Along the Berbera coast, for example, a mosque and a church might each send volunteers to help clear old nets and litter from the beach.
Caring for the sea can be part of a community's shared values, whatever a family believes.
Noticing which groups support a view helps you understand where a local perspective comes from.

bigIdeas.title: Turning an opinion into a reasoned argument
lines: Start with the opinion: what do you think?
Add the reason: because ...
Add the evidence: my count, the report, the record shows ...
A view built this way is one others must take seriously, even if they disagree.

bigIdeas.title: Signal words for cause and consequence
lines: Words that signal a cause: because, since, due to, as a result of, the reason is, caused by.
Words that signal a consequence: so, therefore, as a result, this means that, consequently, this leads to.
When you read a source, underline these words. They point straight to the reasons and the effects.

bigIdeas.title: Graphs as evidence
lines: A bar graph presents research findings clearly and can support an argument.
A double-bar graph lets you compare two groups, such as two years or two seasons.
Always read the title and labels first, or the bars can mislead you.
Add a line of text under any graph to say what pattern it shows and why it matters.

bigIdeas.title: Closed and open-ended questions
lines: Closed question, easy to count: Do you think the catch has fallen in the last five years? Yes or No.
Open-ended question, rich in detail: Why do you think the catch has changed?
Use closed questions for numbers and a graph; use open-ended questions to understand a perspective.
A good questionnaire uses some of each, and never leads people towards one answer.

bigIdeas.title: How to spot a frame
lines: Look for strong words that carry blame or praise, such as greedy, lazy, heroic or disastrous.
Ask what the wording leaves out, and who it makes look good or bad.
Try to restate the issue in plain, neutral words, then compare that with the framed version.
Spotting the frame does not mean the source is lying; it means you can think for yourself.

bigIdeas.title: Questions to ask before you act
lines: What is the issue, stated plainly?
Why is the issue important, and to whom?
Who does the issue affect, and who could help?
Which resources would an action need?
When is action needed, and how urgent is it?
How will I know whether my action has actually helped?

A course of action is worth suggesting only when it is realistic and it fits the issue: a local issue usually needs a local action. A good course of action also has a clear outcome, something people can see or do, such as a poster or presentation to raise awareness, a letter to persuade a leader, or an event to bring people together. Aim for something a learner could really begin, not a grand plan no one could carry out.

bigIdeas.title: Watch out for bias
lines: Bias is when a source or a person leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
A view is not automatically wrong because it takes a side, but you should notice the side and the framing.
Balance a strong view from one group by finding an equally strong, evidence-based view from another.
Being fair does not mean having no opinion. It means forming your opinion only after hearing many sides.

bigIdeas.title: The three questions of analysis
lines: Whenever you feel stuck, come back to these three simple questions.
What is going on? Name the issue clearly and plainly.
Why, and who sees it how? Find the causes and the different perspectives.
So what should happen? Follow the consequences and justify an action.
Every tool in this file helps you answer one of these three questions.

bigIdeas.title: Remember
lines: Facts give you solid ground; opinions tell you how people feel.
A reasoned argument is an opinion you can test, because it shows its reasons and evidence.
A perspective is only worth much when it is supported by evidence.

bigIdeas.title: Signal words to look for
lines: Cause words: because, since, due to, as a result of, the reason is, caused by.
Consequence words: so, therefore, as a result, this means that, consequently, this leads to.
Underline these in any source; they point straight to causes and effects.

bigIdeas.title: Closed and open-ended questions
lines: Closed question: has a yes or no answer, so it is easy to count and to show on a graph.
Open-ended question: invites detail, and often starts with Why or How.
Use some of each, and never lead people towards one answer.
Example closed: Has the catch fallen in five years? Example open: Why do you think it has changed?

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Choose one real issue to analyse across this whole unit. This is your Challenge.
You may keep the issue you researched in Unit 1, or pick a new one where thoughtful people disagree.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you genuinely care about.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It is clear about what it is asking, and short enough to answer quickly.
Closed questions have a yes or no answer, so they are easy to count and to show on a graph.
Open-ended questions invite detail and often start with Why or How.
It is never leading. A leading question pushes people toward one answer, such as: Do you agree the fishers are greedy?

models.title: Analysis happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine the price of fish at the market suddenly doubles one week.
Research would ask: is it dear at every stall, or only one? Has it happened before?
Analysis goes further. It asks why: perhaps the catch was small, or fuel for the boats cost more, or a big buyer took most of the fish.
It asks about consequences on others: families eat less fish, the cafe raises its prices, and a fisher who cannot sell cheaply may earn less.
It asks about perspectives: the fisher, the seller and the shopper would each explain the price in a different way.
Working all of that out, not just noticing the higher price, is analysis. You already do it.

So analysis is not a strange, school-only activity. It is the careful thinking you use whenever you want to understand *why* something is the way it is, and what should be done about it. This unit simply teaches you to do it on purpose, and about issues that matter to your community.

models.title: Zane's example: sorting the three
lines: Issue: the fish catch near Berbera is falling, and it may need action.
Perspective from Mr Diallo, the old fisher: too many boats are taking young fish before they can breed.
Perspective from a younger fisher: the sea simply has good and bad years, and this is a bad one.
Course of action: agree a short rest period each year when no one fishes the breeding grounds.
Notice there is one issue, two perspectives on it, and a separate course of action. None of them is the same kind of thing as the others.

models.title: Zane's example: the falling catch at four perspectives
lines: Personal: Zane thinks the catch is falling mainly because there are far more boats than there were, and he can back this with the harbour records.
Local: many families in Berbera depend on fishing for food and income, so the town views a smaller catch as a threat to its livelihood.
National: the country sees its long coast as a resource for the whole nation, and may pass laws about who may fish and how.
Global: overfishing is a worldwide issue, and organisations across many countries warn that seas fished too hard do not recover quickly.
It is the same sea, seen four ways. Each perspective adds something the others miss.

models.title: Zane's example: three sources on the harbour
lines: Source one, an interview with Mr Diallo: the catch is down because there are too many boats and the young fish are taken too soon.
Source two, a short report from the fisheries office: catches along the whole coast have dropped over five years.
Source three, a message from a boat-fuel seller: business is fine and there is no real problem.

Agreement: Mr Diallo and the report agree the catch is falling. Disagreement: the fuel seller denies it. What is left out: the fuel seller says nothing about the fish records, and Mr Diallo says little about rising costs.
By comparing all three, Zane sees not just the numbers but who benefits from telling the story a certain way.

Comparing is not about deciding at once who is right. It is about mapping the ground carefully first. Once you can see clearly where the sources meet and part, and where the evidence is strongest, you are in a far stronger position to reach a fair conclusion later.

models.title: Nadia's example: sorting three statements
lines: Nadia is analysing what students drink at school.
Fact: on Monday she counted eighteen sugary drinks and seven waters in her class. This can be checked.
Opinion: a classmate says sugary drinks are simply the best, and water is boring. This is a feeling.
Reasoned argument: Nadia argues that sugary drinks should cost more at the shop, because her counts show most students choose them, and the clinic links them to tooth decay.
Nadia keeps all three, but treats her reasoned argument as the strongest, because its reasons and evidence can be tested.

models.title: Zane's example: the chain behind the falling catch
lines: Causes: more boats now fish the same waters; nets with small holes catch young fish before they breed; and higher demand from the growing town pushes everyone to catch more.
Consequences: therefore fewer fish remain; so the catch each day is smaller; as a result fishers stay out longer and spend more on fuel.
The chain onto others: smaller catches raise the market price, so families eat less fish, and Ms Chen's cafe struggles, and some young fishers give up and leave for the city.
Zane maps the whole chain, showing how one cause at sea reaches all the way to a family's evening meal.

models.title: Idris's example: charcoal and the land
lines: Idris is analysing why the soil near his village washes away in the rains.
Cause: because trees are cut for charcoal, the ground is left bare.
Consequence on others: as a result, rain carries the loose soil away, so farmers downhill lose good land and grow less food.
One person's fuel becomes another person's failed harvest. That is a consequence on others.

models.title: Zane's example: a double-bar graph of the catch
lines: Zane collects the harbour records for four months, comparing five years ago with this year, in baskets landed on an average day.
He draws a double-bar graph: for each month, one bar for five years ago and one for this year, so the two can be compared.
The pattern is clear at a glance. This year's bars are lower in every month, and the gap is widest in the calm season, when fishing is easiest.
The graph does not merely show numbers. It supports Zane's argument that the catch is genuinely falling, not just having one unlucky week.

Before you study a graph closely, it is a good habit to make a prediction: a statement of what you think the data will show, or what you think is causing it. Then you check the graph against your prediction. Whether you were right or wrong, you learn something, and comparing your guess with the real pattern is analysis in action.

models.title: Zane's example: who are the stakeholders?
lines: Fishers, whose income depends on the catch.
Fish sellers at the market, who need a steady supply to earn.
Families in Berbera, who rely on fish as affordable food.
Cafe and restaurant owners, such as Ms Chen, who buy fish every day.
The fisheries office, which may set rules for the coast.
The children of fishing families, whose future work is at stake.
Even within one group there are differences: an older fisher may want rest periods, while a younger one, needing money now, may resist them.

To gather a group's perspective fairly, Stage 8 researchers often design a short questionnaire. Mix two kinds of question. Closed questions have a yes or no answer; they are quick and easy to count and to show on a graph. Open-ended questions invite more than a yes or no, so people can explain themselves; they often begin with 'Why' or 'How', and you summarise the replies in a paragraph.

models.title: Zane's example: three frames, one harbour
lines: Frame one: 'Greedy fishers are stripping our sea bare.' This blames the fishers and hides their hardship.
Frame two: 'Hard-working families can no longer feed the town.' This wins sympathy and hides any overfishing.
Frame three: 'A shared resource is being used faster than it can recover.' This is cooler and points towards agreed rules.
Zane notices that all three describe the same falling catch, but each pushes him towards a different reaction. He tries to state the issue plainly, without a frame, before he judges.

models.title: Zane's example: from analysis to a justified action
lines: Conclusion, built on evidence: the catch is genuinely falling; the records show a five-year drop, most fishers and the fisheries office agree, and the main causes are too many boats and nets that take young fish.
His questions: the issue is urgent for fishing families now; the fishers and the fisheries office could act together; the main resource needed is agreement.
Course of action: propose a short annual rest period for the breeding grounds, plus larger net holes to spare young fish.
Outcome: a clear presentation to the fishers' meeting and a poster for the market, so the plan is understood and discussed.
The action is local, realistic, and tied straight to the causes Zane found. That is what makes it justified, not just well-meant.

You will not solve a whole issue in one unit, and that is fine. The skill is to reach a fair, evidence-based conclusion and justify a sensible next step. That honest, careful judgement is the true goal of Analysis.

models.title: Zane's whole journey, from a falling catch to a plan
lines: Skill 1: he separated the issue, the falling catch, from the perspectives on it and the actions to fix it.
Skill 2: he viewed the sea through personal, local, national and global perspectives.
Skills 3 and 4: he compared three sources and sorted their facts, opinions and reasoned arguments.
Skill 5: he mapped the causes and followed the consequences onto families and the cafe.
Skill 6: he built a double-bar graph of the catch to support his argument.
Skills 7 and 8: he listed every stakeholder and noticed how the issue was being framed.
Skill 9: he reached an evidence-based conclusion and justified a rest period and larger net holes.

By following this cycle, Zane turned a worried feeling about the harbour into clear thinking and a sensible plan. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle on your own Challenge issue, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck: cutting trees for charcoal
lines: Personal: I think cutting too many trees is harming our land, and the bare hillsides after rain are my evidence.
Local: our village depends on charcoal for cooking and for income, so views here are divided.
National: the country may pass laws to protect forests and control charcoal.
Global: cutting trees adds to climate change, which affects every country.

models.title: A model: three views on the falling catch
lines: Source one, a fisher: the catch is down because there are too many boats.
Source two, the fisheries office report: catches have dropped across five years.
Source three, a fuel seller: there is no real problem, business is fine.
Agreement: the fisher and the report agree the catch is falling. Missing: the fuel seller ignores the records, because admitting the problem would not suit his trade.

models.title: A model: Zara turns an opinion into a reasoned argument
lines: Opinion: Zara says the buses in Hargeisa are hopeless.
Add a reason: because they are often too full to board.
Add evidence: on three mornings she counted two full buses pass before she could get on.
Reasoned argument: the buses are not serving people well, because they are often too full to board; on three mornings Zara watched two full buses pass before she could get on.

models.title: A model: the falling catch
lines: Issue in the centre: the fish catch is falling.
Causes: because there are more boats; because small-holed nets take young fish; because the town's demand keeps rising.
Consequences: as a result, fewer fish remain, so the daily catch shrinks and fuel costs rise.
Chain onto others: a smaller catch raises the price, so families eat less fish and the cafe owner cannot buy enough.

When your map is done, turn it into a short spoken commentary: two or three sentences naming the issue, its main cause, and one consequence that lands on other people. Saying it aloud helps you explain the chain clearly, which you will need for your conclusion.

models.title: A model: three frames of one issue
lines: Blaming frame: greedy fishers are stripping our sea bare.
Sympathetic frame: hard-working families can no longer feed the town.
Neutral frame: the fish catch has fallen over the last five years.
The strong words greedy and hard-working do the steering; the neutral version simply states what can be checked.

models.title: A model: Zane's conclusion and action
lines: Evidence: the records show a five-year fall; the fisheries office and most fishers agree; the main causes are too many boats and small-holed nets.
Conclusion: the falling catch is a genuine, shared problem with causes that people could act on.
Course of action: propose an annual rest period for the breeding grounds and larger net holes.
How the evidence justifies it: because the causes are known and most fishers agree, an agreed rest period is realistic and aimed straight at the cause.

toolkit.title: The analysis cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your issue, strong Stage 8 analysis follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Name the issue: state the problem plainly, apart from any one view of it.
Use the four perspectives: view it personally, locally, nationally and globally.
Gather across sources: compare perspectives, and sort fact, opinion and reasoned argument.
Find causes and consequences: ask why it happens and what it leads to, for others too.
Read and build data: find patterns, and list the stakeholders who care.
Notice the framing: see how the wording steers you, and restate it plainly.
Conclude and justify action: reach an evidence-based judgement and a realistic step.

toolkit.title: The Analysis skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it better. Instead of treating a problem as one solid lump, you ask careful questions about the pieces inside it: What exactly is the issue? Why is it happening (causes)? What does it lead to, and for whom (consequences)? Who is involved, and how does each of them see it (perspectives)? Then you bring the pieces together into a fair, supported conclusion.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always look for more than one perspective, because every issue looks different depending on who is standing where. Second, always ask for the evidence behind a view, so you never mistake a bare opinion for a reasoned argument or a proven fact. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 8 Analysis objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong analysis looks like at this stage. Here are the official Stage 8 Analysis objectives, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: Identify ideas and evidence from different perspectives within different sources on a given topic.
Find the different points of view inside several sources, and the evidence behind each one.
Explain how graphical or numerical data supports an argument.
Read or build a graph or set of numbers, spot the pattern, and use it to back up a point.
Explain causes of a local or global issue and consequences on others.
Say why an issue happens and follow its effects onto other people.
Suggest and justify different actions to make a positive difference to a national or global issue.
Suggest a realistic action to help, with a clear outcome, and give good reasons for it.

toolkit.title: Issue, perspective and course of action
toolkit.intro: Quick test: if people might say 'someone should do something about this', it is an issue. If you can put 'I think' in front of it, it is a perspective. If it starts with a verb like 'organise' or 'ask', it is a course of action.

rows: Issue
An important topic or problem that people care about and that may need a solution.
Fewer fish, waste, traffic, water.
Perspective
A way of looking at an issue, shaped by who someone is and where they live.
Too many boats are to blame; the sea just has bad years.
Course of action
Something you could do to make a positive difference to the issue.
Agree a rest period; write to the fisheries office.

toolkit.title: Template: An issue through four perspectives
toolkit.intro: Copy this table for your issue. Fill in how the issue looks from each perspective. It stops you from thinking too narrowly.

rows: Personal
What do I think, and what evidence is my view based on?
Local
How does my community view this issue?
National
How might my country view it, through its laws or leaders?
Global
How does this issue reach beyond any one country?

toolkit.title: Sorter: Fact, opinion or reasoned argument?
toolkit.intro: Hold any statement up against these questions before you rely on it.
items: Can it be checked or measured? If yes, it is a fact.
Is it a bare belief that others could dispute, with no reason given? That is an opinion.
Does it give an opinion plus a reason plus evidence? That is a reasoned argument, the strongest of the three.
If it is only an opinion, ask: what reason and what evidence would turn it into a reasoned argument?

toolkit.title: Template: Cause-and-consequence chain
toolkit.intro: Put your issue in the middle row. List the causes and the consequences, then follow the chain, showing how one consequence becomes a cause of trouble for someone else.

rows: Causes (why it happens)
The issue
Consequences (what it leads to)
Chain onto others (a consequence that causes a new problem, and for whom)

toolkit.title: Template: Compare perspectives across sources
toolkit.intro: Use this grid to compare two or three sources. The 'what is missing' row is often the most revealing.

rows: What perspective does it give?
What evidence does it offer?
Where does it agree with the others?
What does it leave out, and who does that suit?

toolkit.title: Data-reading guide
toolkit.intro:
Read a graph in this order so it cannot mislead you.

A bar graph presents findings clearly and supports an argument. A double-bar graph compares two groups side by side, such as two years, two seasons, or two places. Always add a sentence of text to say what a graph shows and why it matters.
items: Read the title: what is the graph about?
Read the labels on each axis: what is counted, and in what units?
Look at the bars: which is tallest, which is shortest?
Name the pattern: what is the overall story?
Ask why: what might have caused the pattern?

toolkit.title: Template: Stakeholders and questions
toolkit.intro: List every group with an interest in your issue and what each cares about most. Remember that perspectives can differ even inside one group. Then design a few questions to gather one group's perspective.

toolkit.title: The conclusion and course-of-action frame
toolkit.intro:
When your analysis is done, use these questions to move from a messy issue to a justified action.

A good course of action is realistic, fits the size of the issue (a local issue needs a local action), and has a clear outcome, such as a poster, a presentation, a letter, or an event.
items: What is the issue, stated plainly?
Why is it important, and to whom?
Who does it affect, and who could help?
Which resources would an action need?
When is action needed, and how urgent is it?
How will I know whether my action has helped?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for analysis
toolkit.intro: Use these to write clear analysis. Mix and match them as you need.

toolkit.title: For causes and consequences:
items: This happens because ...
One cause of this is ...
As a result of this, ...
This leads to ... which then affects ...

toolkit.title: For perspectives and comparing:
items: From a personal / local / national / global perspective, ...
One source sees this as ... while another sees it as ...
Both sources agree that ... but they differ on ...
This source leaves out ...

toolkit.title: For conclusions and actions:
items: The evidence suggests that ...
Weighing all the perspectives, I conclude that ...
One realistic action would be ... because ...
This action fits the issue because ...

checklists.title: Checklist: Spotting the framing
checklists.intro: The same issue can be worded to steer how people feel. Before you judge a statement, run this check.
items: Look for strong words that carry blame or praise, such as greedy, lazy, heroic or disastrous.
Ask what the wording leaves out, and who it makes look good or bad.
Restate the issue in plain, neutral words, with no blame and no praise.
Compare the neutral version with the framed one to see how the framing was steering you.

challenge.intro: Look back at the issue list in the Lesson file (fewer fish, clean air and traffic, growing towns, charcoal and trees, plastic waste, road safety, girls in school, work for young people, water and sanitation). Choose one that matters where you live, or continue with your Unit 1 topic. The best issue for analysis is one where different people would honestly say different things.
topics: Write your chosen issue in one sentence: 'The issue I am analysing is ...'.
Write one reason it matters to you personally.
Name two people or groups who might see this issue very differently from each other.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Issue, perspective or course of action?
activities.label: Activity 2: Issue, perspective or course of action?
activities.intro:
Remember the three-way difference: an issue is a problem that may need action, a perspective is a way of looking at it, and a course of action is something you could do about it. Sort the nine statements below into three columns with those headings.

Write each letter under the right heading. Then, in one sentence of your own, explain the difference between a perspective and a course of action, because these two are the easiest to confuse.
steps: A. The fish catch near the coast is falling.
B. Organise a yearly rest period for the breeding grounds.
C. Too many boats are taking young fish before they breed.
D. Plastic waste on the beach.

F. The sea just has good years and bad years.
G. Road safety near the school.

I. Hold a clean-up day and put up a poster.

activities.title: Compare perspectives across sources
activities.label: Activity 4: Compare perspectives across sources
activities.intro:
Find or imagine three sources with different perspectives on your issue, for example a person affected, a report, and someone who benefits from the current situation. Set them side by side and compare.

The 'missing' question is the most interesting. What a source stays silent about often shows what its perspective would rather you did not think about.
steps: Write each source's perspective in one or two sentences.
Agreement: where do any of the sources agree?
Disagreement: where do they clash?
Missing: what does each source leave out, and who does that silence suit?

boxes.title: A model: three views on the falling catch
lines: Source one, a fisher: the catch is down because there are too many boats.

activities.title: Fact, opinion or reasoned argument?
activities.label: Activity 5: Fact, opinion or reasoned argument?
activities.intro:
A good analyst sorts three kinds of statement: a fact can be checked, an opinion is a bare belief, and a reasoned argument is an opinion backed by reasons and evidence. Read the six statements below and label each one F, O or R.

Write F, O or R next to each letter. Then take one statement you marked O and turn it into a reasoned argument by adding a reason and a piece of evidence.
steps: A. Last month the harbour recorded twenty-two baskets landed on an average day.
B. The sea is simply empty now, and that is that.
C. The catch has halved in five years because there are more boats and the young fish are netted too soon.
D. Fishing is the best job in the world.
E. More than thirty motorbikes passed the school gate in ten minutes.

boxes.title: A model: Zara turns an opinion into a reasoned argument
lines: Opinion: Zara says the buses in Hargeisa are hopeless.
Add a reason: because they are often too full to board.

Reasoned argument: the buses are not serving people well, because they are often too full to board; on three mornings Zara watched two full buses pass before she could get on.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six labels to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.

activities.title: Map the cause-and-consequence chain
activities.label: Activity 6: Map the cause-and-consequence chain
activities.intro: Put your issue in the middle. On one side list its causes (why it happens); on the other list its consequences (what it leads to). Then follow the chain, showing how one consequence becomes a cause of trouble for someone else. Use the signal words: because and due to point to causes; so and as a result point to consequences.
steps: Write your issue in the centre of a page.
On the left, write two or three causes. Start each with 'This happens because ...'.
On the right, write two or three consequences. Start each with 'As a result, ...'.
Draw an arrow from a consequence that becomes the cause of a new problem for another group, and name that group.

lines: Issue in the centre: the fish catch is falling.

When your map is done, turn it into a short spoken commentary: two or three sentences naming the issue, its main cause, and one consequence that lands on other people. Saying it aloud helps you explain the chain clearly, which you will need for your conclusion.

activities.label: Activity 7: Read and build the data
activities.intro:
Data can make an argument strong. Below is a small set of numbers from Zane's Challenge. It shows the baskets of fish landed on an average day, comparing five years ago with this year, across four months. Read it carefully, then answer the questions.

Now analyse the data:

Before you check with your tutor, make a prediction: if nothing changes, what do you think next year's numbers would look like, and why?
steps: In which month was the fall in the catch the largest?
What overall pattern do you notice between the two years?
Write one sentence that uses this data to support the argument that the catch is falling.

April
July

Ask it whether you spotted the main pattern and used the data fairly.

activities.title: Map stakeholders and design a questionnaire
activities.label: Activity 8: Map stakeholders and design a questionnaire
activities.intro: A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in your issue. First map them, then design a short questionnaire to gather one group's perspective fairly.
steps: Write your issue in the centre of a page, and around it write every stakeholder group you can think of, at least five.
For each group, write one word or phrase for what they care about most.
Choose one group whose perspective you want to understand better.
Write two closed questions (yes or no) and two open-ended questions (starting with Why or How) to gather that group's perspective.

boxes.title: What makes a good questionnaire question
lines: It is clear about what it is asking, and short enough to answer quickly.
Closed questions have a yes or no answer, so they are easy to count and to show on a graph.
Open-ended questions invite detail and often start with Why or How.
It is never leading. A leading question pushes people toward one answer, such as: Do you agree the fishers are greedy?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your stakeholder map and your four questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: are any of my questions leading or unclear, and how would you fix them?
Ask the tutor whether my questions would really reveal this group's perspective.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: With a trusted adult's help, ask your questionnaire to a few people from that stakeholder group.
Count the answers to your closed questions, and note the replies to your open-ended ones.
Bring your findings to your next teacher session and compare them with what you expected.

activities.title: Spot the framing
activities.label: Activity 9: Spot the framing
activities.intro: The same issue can be framed in different ways, and the wording quietly steers how people feel. Practise noticing the frame and stating the issue plainly.
steps: Take your Challenge issue and write it in a frame that blames one group, using strong words.
Now write it in a frame that wins sympathy for that same group.
Now write it in plain, neutral words, with no blame and no praise.
Write one sentence about which words changed, and how each frame made you feel.

boxes.title: A model: three frames of one issue
lines: Blaming frame: greedy fishers are stripping our sea bare.
Sympathetic frame: hard-working families can no longer feed the town.
Neutral frame: the fish catch has fallen over the last five years.
The strong words greedy and hard-working do the steering; the neutral version simply states what can be checked.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three frames to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your neutral version really is free of blame and praise.
Then ask the tutor to show you a frame on my issue that I had not thought of, and who it would suit.

activities.title: Draw a conclusion and justify an action
activities.label: Activity 10: Draw a conclusion and justify an action
activities.intro: Now bring your whole analysis together. A strong conclusion rests on evidence, the causes, consequences, data and perspectives you have gathered, not on how you feel. Keep your cause map, your comparison, your data and your stakeholder list beside you.
steps: Write down the three strongest pieces of evidence from your analysis so far.
Write one conclusion that those pieces of evidence support.
Use the What, Why, Who, Which, When and How questions to think through a possible action.
Suggest one realistic course of action that fits your issue, with a clear outcome (a poster, a presentation, a letter, an event), and write one sentence saying how your evidence justifies it.

boxes.title: A model: Zane's conclusion and action
lines: Evidence: the records show a five-year fall; the fisheries office and most fishers agree; the main causes are too many boats and small-holed nets.
Conclusion: the falling catch is a genuine, shared problem with causes that people could act on.
Course of action: propose an annual rest period for the breeding grounds and larger net holes.
How the evidence justifies it: because the causes are known and most fishers agree, an agreed rest period is realistic and aimed straight at the cause.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your evidence, conclusion and course of action to your AI tutor.
Ask it: is my conclusion really supported by my evidence, or am I jumping ahead?
Ask the tutor whether my course of action is realistic, fits the size of my issue, and has a clear outcome.

activities.title: Looking ahead
activities.label: Looking ahead
activities.intro: Everything you have taken apart in this unit is the raw material for the rest of your Global Perspectives year. In the next unit, Evaluation, you will weigh the perspectives and arguments you have gathered and judge how strong each one really is. Keep your analysis journal, your data and your stakeholder list safe, because you will reach for them again.

boxes.title: Share your progress
lines: Bring your cause map, your data and your conclusion to your next teacher session.
Tell your teacher which perspective on your issue surprised you the most, and why.
Ask them one question about your Challenge that your analysis has not yet answered.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'analysis' mean?
practice.answer: Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it, by asking why it happens, what it leads to, and how different people see it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: What is the difference between an issue, a perspective and a course of action?
practice.answer: An issue is a problem that may need action; a perspective is a way of looking at that issue; a course of action is something you could do about it.

practice.prompt: Name the four perspective types you can use to look at an issue.
practice.answer: Personal, local, national and global.

practice.prompt: True or false: a personal perspective should be based on evidence, not just a feeling.
practice.answer: True. A personal perspective must be based on evidence, or it is only an opinion.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between an opinion and a reasoned argument?
practice.answer: An opinion is a bare belief; a reasoned argument is an opinion backed by reasons and evidence, so it can be tested.

practice.prompt: A ______ is the reason why something happens; a ______ is the result of something happening.
practice.answer: A cause is the reason why something happens; a consequence is the result.

practice.prompt: Give one signal word that points to a cause, and one that points to a consequence.
practice.answer: Cause word: any of because, since, due to, as a result of. Consequence word: any of so, therefore, as a result, consequently.

practice.prompt: What is a stakeholder?
practice.answer: A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them or they can affect it.

practice.prompt: True or false: everyone in the same stakeholder group always shares exactly the same perspective.
practice.answer: False. Even within one group there can be different perspectives.

practice.prompt: Which kind of graph lets you compare two groups, such as two years, side by side?
practice.answer: A double-bar graph.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between a closed question and an open-ended question?
practice.answer: A closed question has a yes or no answer and is easy to count; an open-ended question invites more detail and often starts with Why or How.

practice.prompt: When someone words an issue to steer how you feel about it, what is that called?
practice.answer: Framing (or wording the issue to steer how people feel).

practice.prompt: A national perspective is often seen in a country's ______, policies and the speeches of its politicians.
practice.answer: Laws.

practice.prompt: Give one of the six question words used to think through a course of action.
practice.answer: Any one of: What, Why, Who, Which, When, How.

practice.prompt: Why should a conclusion be supported by evidence and not just by your feelings?
practice.answer: Because a conclusion based only on feelings can be unfair or wrong; evidence makes it trustworthy and lets others check it.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each analysis word (1 to 8) to the correct meaning (A to H). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Issue
options: A. A way of looking at an issue, a point of view.
B. An opinion backed by clear reasons and evidence.
C. A problem or important topic that people care about and that may need action.
D. Wording an issue so as to steer how people feel about it.
E. Anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them.
F. Something you could do to make a positive difference to an issue.
G. A chart that compares two groups side by side.
H. The result or effect of something that has happened.
practice.answer: C — A problem or important topic that people care about and that may need action.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Perspective
practice.answer: A — A way of looking at an issue, a point of view.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Course of action
practice.answer: F — Something you could do to make a positive difference to an issue.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Reasoned argument
practice.answer: B — An opinion backed by clear reasons and evidence.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Consequence
practice.answer: H — The result or effect of something that has happened.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Stakeholder
practice.answer: E — Anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Framing
practice.answer: D — Wording an issue so as to steer how people feel about it.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Double-bar graph
practice.answer: G — A chart that compares two groups side by side.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Zane reads: 'The catch has halved in five years because there are more boats and the young fish are netted too soon.' Is this a fact, a bare opinion, or a reasoned argument? How can you tell?
practice.answer: A reasoned argument. It gives an opinion (the catch has halved) plus reasons and evidence (more boats, young fish netted too soon) that can be checked.

practice.prompt: A fisher says rest periods are needed, while a fuel seller says there is no problem. What is the issue, and what are the two perspectives?
practice.answer: The issue is the falling fish catch. The two perspectives are the fisher's (rest periods are needed) and the fuel seller's (there is no problem).

practice.prompt: Idris writes: 'Because trees are cut for charcoal, the soil washes away, so farmers downhill lose land.' Name the cause, the consequence, and the group the consequence lands on.
practice.answer: Cause: trees are cut for charcoal. Consequence: the soil washes away. The consequence lands on the farmers downhill, who lose land.

practice.prompt: Yasmin is analysing why some girls in Mogadishu leave school early. Give one personal-level view and one national-level view of this issue.
practice.answer: Personal view: a girl or her family weighing school against work at home. National view: the country may have laws or policies to keep girls in school. (Other sensible answers are fine.)

practice.prompt: Karim reads a headline that calls the fishers 'greedy'. What is this technique called, and how should a fair analyst respond?
practice.answer: It is called framing. A fair analyst notices the strong word, states the issue in neutral terms, and looks at the evidence before judging.

practice.prompt: Nadia's double-bar graph shows sugary drinks far higher than water every day. Write one sentence using her data to support an argument.
practice.answer: Example: 'On every day of the week, students brought far more sugary drinks than water, which supports the argument that water should be made easier to choose.'

practice.prompt: Two shopkeepers in the same market disagree about an issue. Does this prove that one stakeholder group always shares one perspective? Explain.
practice.answer: No. Two shopkeepers in one group disagreeing shows that a single stakeholder group can hold different perspectives.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Working with my AI tutor, my discussion partner ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Asking a family member or neighbour for their perspective ...
Mapping my ideas, such as causes, perspectives and stakeholders, on paper ...

vocabulary.meaning: Breaking an issue into parts to understand it, by asking why, what it leads to, and how people see it.
An important topic or problem that people care about and that may need a solution.
A way of looking at an issue, shaped by who someone is and where they live.
Your own view of an issue, based on evidence, which can change as you learn more.
The view a particular community holds about an issue.
The view a whole country takes, seen in its laws, policies and politicians' speeches.
A view whose influence spreads beyond any single country.
Something you could do to make a positive difference to an issue.
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may dispute.
An opinion backed by clear reasons and evidence, so it can be tested.
Facts or information that support an idea or a view.
The reason why an event or situation happens or has happened.
The result or effect of something that has happened or is happening.
The way an effect ripples out to touch other people.
A word that points to a cause or a consequence, such as because or therefore.
Information in the form of numbers, counts or measurements.
A chart that shows amounts as bars, useful for presenting findings.
A bar graph that compares two groups side by side.
A repeated or overall shape in data that tells you something.
A statement of what you think will happen or what the data will show.
Anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them or they can affect it.
A question with a yes or no answer, easy to count and to graph.
A question that invites detail, often starting with Why or How.
Wording an issue so as to steer how people feel about it.
When a source or person leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
A careful judgement reached after weighing the evidence and perspectives.
The visible result of a course of action, such as a poster, presentation or letter.
Actually useful for understanding your particular issue.
A short spoken or written explanation of an issue, its cause and its consequence.

mistakes: Describing only your own perspective and forgetting the others.
Treating a bare opinion as if it were a reasoned argument or a proven fact.
Naming a cause but forgetting the consequences, or the effects on other people.
Getting stuck at one perspective, such as only the personal or only the global.
Comparing sources but never asking what each one leaves out.
Reading only the bars of a graph without checking the title and labels.
Being steered by a frame without noticing it, or jumping to a conclusion before the evidence.

selfAssessment.statement: I can tell apart an issue, a perspective and a course of action.
I can view an issue through personal, local, national and global perspectives.
I can identify and compare perspectives across several sources.
I can sort fact, opinion and reasoned argument.
I can explain the causes of an issue and its consequences on others.
I can read and build data, such as a double-bar graph, to support an argument.
I can identify stakeholders and design questions to gather a group's perspective.
I can notice how an issue is framed and restate it plainly.
I can draw an evidence-based conclusion and justify a realistic course of action.
